A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CLCIFAR dataset study and annotation protocol. All 13 pages of v1 and 22 pages of v2 are readable, including v2's Appendices A–F. Corresponding experiments, tables, and figures can be matched across their reorganization.

before.justification: Sections 4–5 report original human-annotation statistics, classification benchmarks, validation comparisons, and noise-cleaning and multiple-label experiments.

after.justification: Sections 4–5 retain original annotation and benchmark results, while Appendices A–C report additional noise, robust-loss, augmentation, and interpolation experiments.

M1.justification: The collection protocol and model architecture are retained. Appendix B.2 introduces a limited FWD adaptation using an interpolated transition matrix, alpha Tu + (1-alpha) Te, extending v1's experiments with the uniform and empirical matrices separately.

E1.justification: v2 adds uniformly noisy synthetic-label scenarios through Section 5.4 and CLCIFAR10-N/CLCIFAR20-N in Appendix A.2. The underlying CIFAR images and classification tasks remain unchanged. The human-label, uniform noiseless, empirical-matrix-resampled, noise-cleaned, and multiple-label scenarios already existed in v1.

E2.justification: v2 adds a substantial comparison group targeting noisy complementary labels: CCE, MAE, WMAE, GCE, and SL. MAE appears in Table 1 and the full group in Appendix A. The original nine comparator variants, including PC-sigmoid, were already evaluated in v1.

E3.justification: The principal synthetic-versus-human comparison changes: v1 explicitly excluded uniform-CIFAR from augmentation, whereas v2 applies augmentation in the standard synthetic benchmarks. v2 also introduces controlled uniform-noise injection and transition-matrix interpolation protocols. ResNet-18, Adam, the 300-epoch budget, batch size, and learning-rate grid are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds a uniform-noise control to separate noise from bias, synthetic-versus-practical-noise analysis, and interpolation-based regularization experiments. It expands augmentation analysis with training curves and noise-cleaning analysis beyond FWD in Appendix C. The validation and multiple-label studies largely retain existing evidence despite relocation.

E5.justification: Both versions report four-seed means and standard deviations for the main benchmarks. v2 additionally reports standard deviations of IID-versus-human accuracy differences in Table 2. Conversely, retained unaugmented synthetic scores in Table 7 omit their former standard deviations, and Table 3 drops its explicit four-trial averaging statement.

E6.justification: v2 adds augmented synthetic results, robust-loss scores, and noise/interpolation findings. For example, Table 1 reports FWD-U at 69.17% on augmented uniform-CIFAR10 versus v1's 48.44% without augmentation; this is not a same-setting gain. Existing human-label, validation, and multiple-label scores are largely retained. The unaugmented CLCIFAR10 FWD-U value changes from 21.9 in v1 Table 2 to 21.29 in v2 Table 7.

T1.justification: Appendices A.2 and B.2 introduce mathematical constructions for the synthetic-noise transition matrix and the interpolated matrix family. Existing CLL assumptions and the URE expression remain unchanged, with no new proofs or guarantees. Equation 2 explicitly documents SCEL, an objective already used in v1.

C1.justification: The dataset-release contribution remains central. v2 explicitly claims the first real-world CLL datasets and sharpens the main empirical takeaway: annotation noise is the dominant performance obstacle, while bias promotes overfitting. v1's abstract and conclusion made broader claims about benchmarking and the effects of noise and nonuniformity.

C2.justification: v2 expands the interpretation into distinct roles for noise, bias, and feature dependence, adds a synthetic-versus-practical-noise explanation for robust-loss failures, and interprets gradient ascent as regularization. Appendix C strengthens the noise-cleaning conclusion to gaps vanishing for all algorithms, although several CLCIFAR20 curves remain below the updated uniform benchmarks in Table 1.

D1.justification: v2 discloses random selection of one collected label per image, a 10% validation holdout, V100/RTX 2070 hardware, and specific augmentation operators. These mostly clarify existing experiments. Appendix F explicitly mentions reproduction code at the retained repository. However, the validation section loses v1's explicit last-epoch/no-early-stopping statement.

R1.justification: v2 retains the earlier CLL references and adds five background works covering weak supervision, noisy labels, partial labels, and positive-unlabeled learning. It also makes the first-real-world-dataset positioning explicit, without replacing the paper's overall research context.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and experimental narrative are substantially rewritten. Section 5 is reorganized around feature dependence, noise, and bias; validation moves later, and multiple-label and overfitting material moves into appendices. Baseline descriptions and explanations, including SCEL, are expanded.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the distribution plots and heatmaps, converts the IID accuracy table into a compact difference table, and reorganizes the noise-cleaning figures between the main text and Appendix C. It relocates existing tables and adds robust-loss/noisy-synthetic tables, augmentation curves, an interpolation plot, and a label-name table.

improvement.justification: Applying augmentation to both sides improves the main benchmark's comparability, while robust-loss comparisons and clearer implementation details address gaps in v1. The net gain is limited by problems in the added material: Appendix A.2 divides the human noise rates by the class count, Table 5 reports a FWD-U difference of 2.2 although 37.10 minus 34.09 is 3.01, and Appendix C overstates universal gap closure. These inconsistencies limit confidence in the expanded interpretations.
